clue.text: Old writer's confusing 'ere'? Google it!

indicators.note: something confusing is muddled up, so the quoted words are jumbled into a new order

explanation.surface: Someone baffled by an archaic word in an old author is told to look it up online.
explanation.walkthrough: The writer is GEORGE ELIOT, pen name of Mary Ann Evans; the dropped-aitch 'ere' is just more letters.
explanation.definitionFit: George Eliot was the Victorian novelist who wrote Middlemarch, so certainly an author from long ago.

clue.text: Tennis champ on football team

parts.note: Chris Evert, multiple Grand Slam singles winner

explanation.surface: A tennis star turns out for a football club.
explanation.walkthrough: EVERTON is a Premier League club from Liverpool.
explanation.definitionFit: Everton is a professional soccer club based in Liverpool, England.

clue.text: Impropriety when sundresses peeled off

indicators.note: off suggests something gone wrong or spoiled, so what remains is rearranged
peeling strips the skin, so the word loses its outermost letter at each end

explanation.surface: Stripping off one's summer frocks is deemed indecent.
explanation.walkthrough: Removing the outer S at each end leaves UNDRESSE, which rearranges to RUDENESS.
explanation.definitionFit: Rudeness is bad manners or offensive conduct, a kind of improper behaviour.

clue.text: Move with gentleness and calm

definitions.meaning: first meaning: to manoeuvre something carefully into place
second meaning: relaxed comfort, freedom from worry

explanation.walkthrough: The clue reads like one instruction, but the verb sense and the noun sense are separate.
explanation.definitionFit: As a verb it means to slide or guide carefully; as a noun it means comfort and freedom from strain.

clue.text: Management of car showroom swapping fronts of De Loreans

indicators.note: swapping means two letters exchange places within the word

parts.note: a dealership is a business that sells cars

indicators.note: fronts are the leading edges, so only the opening letter of each word counts

parts.note: the initials of the two words

explanation.surface: Bosses at a sports-car dealer mix up their DeLorean stock.
explanation.walkthrough: In DEALERSHIP the D and the L change places to make LEADERSHIP. The DeLorean is the stainless-steel car from Back to the Future.
explanation.definitionFit: Leadership means the people directing an organisation, its management team.

clue.text: Group of Aussies regularly falling out

indicators.note: letters fall out at regular intervals, so every other one is dropped

parts.note: first, third, fifth, seventh and ninth letters

explanation.surface: A gang of Australians keep quarrelling.
explanation.walkthrough: OASIS were the Manchester rock band whose Gallagher brothers famously fell out, so the surface fits the answer too.
explanation.definitionFit: Oasis was a 1990s British band, and a band is a musical group.

clue.text: Brother and another; alternately, one of three sisters

indicators.note: alternately means taking every second letter in turn

explanation.surface: Siblings counted off in turn, one belonging to a famous trio of sisters.
explanation.walkthrough: Charlotte, Emily and Anne Bronte were the three novelist sisters of Haworth.
explanation.definitionFit: Charlotte, Emily and Anne shared that surname, so any one of the literary siblings is a Bronte.

clue.text: 'At home with Viscount, I close both eyes.' Earl admitted: 'it's hard to read'

indicators.note: admitted means let inside, so one letter goes within another word

parts.note: Vis. is an abbreviation for Viscount
to blink is to shut both eyes briefly
E is the abbreviation for Earl

explanation.surface: A snippet of aristocratic gossip: a viscount at home, and an earl owning up.
explanation.walkthrough: The earl's letter slips in after the L of the blinking, not around the whole phrase.
explanation.definitionFit: Invisible ink leaves writing that cannot be seen until treated, so it is notoriously difficult to make out.

clue.text: Doss about, eating first piece of picnic in swimming trunks

indicators.note: eating means taking something inside, so one piece swallows another
about suggests being moved around, so the letters of the first word are rearranged
the first piece is the opening letter of the next word

parts.note: the initial letter, spelt out as the name of the letter

explanation.surface: Lazing around at a picnic in swimwear.
explanation.walkthrough: The letter is written out as its name, PEE, which is how dictionaries spell it; it goes after the first S of the rearranged word.
explanation.definitionFit: Speedos is a brand name used generically for tight men's swimwear, i.e. bathing briefs.

clue.text: Wine in gallons, rosé, under sun shade

indicators.note: in a down entry, being under something means coming after it in the column

parts.note: S is the abbreviation for sun
hock is German white wine from the Rhine
G is the abbreviation for gallons

explanation.surface: Plenty of wine and rosé enjoyed in the sunshine.
explanation.walkthrough: Hock is the British name for Rhine wine. In a down entry 'under sun' puts everything else below the S.
explanation.definitionFit: Shocking pink is a vivid magenta colour, and a shade is a particular hue.

clue.text: Meal's orange, peeled twice: this one won't amount to much

definitions.text: this one won't amount to much

indicators.note: peeling twice strips two layers, so the outer two letters at each end of the phrase go

parts.note: the inner letters, with ME and GE stripped off

explanation.surface: A cook peels a dinner's orange over and over, and the result is meagre.
explanation.walkthrough: Everyman pins down the hidden word exactly: two letters come off each end.
explanation.definitionFit: An also-ran is a loser or nonentity, someone unlikely to achieve anything notable.

clue.text: Frequently in temper, losing head

indicators.note: losing its head means the word drops its opening letter

parts.note: to temper is to moderate or make milder

explanation.surface: Someone who regularly loses their head in a rage.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Temper' looks like anger, but it is the verb meaning moderate.
explanation.definitionFit: Often and frequently both mean many times, happening again and again.

clue.text: City's removing 50% of helipads: let that sink in

indicators.note: letting something in places it inside the remaining letters
removing half means taking away four of the eight letters

explanation.surface: A city cutting its heliports in half, with a solemn invitation to reflect on it.
explanation.walkthrough: Removing PADS leaves HELI, and SINK goes in before its last letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Helsinki is the capital of Finland, a major Nordic urban centre.

clue.text: Dancer cavorting with lyre somewhere on high street

indicators.note: cavorting is leaping around wildly, so the letters jump into a new order

explanation.surface: A street performer prancing about with a harp-like instrument in the town centre.
explanation.walkthrough: The high street is the main shopping street of a British town.
explanation.definitionFit: A dry cleaner's is a typical shop found among the stores on a town's main shopping strip.

clue.text: Sings and rocks out somewhere in London

indicators.note: out suggests things put out of place, so the letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: A busker belts out tunes and rocks out in the capital.
explanation.walkthrough: King's Cross is a main-line railway station and district in north London.
explanation.definitionFit: King's Cross is a district and major station in central London, so a specific place there.

clue.text: Where to get meat in Indian city, they say

indicators.note: they say means as people pronounce it, so sound matters rather than spelling

parts.note: Delhi is the Indian capital region

explanation.surface: Shopping for meat in an Indian metropolis.
explanation.definitionFit: A delicatessen sells cooked and cured meats, cheeses and prepared foods.

clue.text: Drama when a republican expelled from Green Party organisation

indicators.note: organisation means arranging, so the remaining letters are put into a fresh order
expelled from means thrown out, so those letters leave the phrase

parts.note: R is the abbreviation for republican

explanation.surface: Political drama as a republican is thrown out of the Green Party.
explanation.walkthrough: Taking A and one R out of GREENPARTY leaves GEENPTRY, which rearranges to the title.
explanation.definitionFit: Peer Gynt is Ibsen's verse play, a classic piece of theatre.

clue.text: Stupefied, having taken umbrage a little

indicators.note: a little means only a small portion of the words is taken

explanation.surface: Someone stunned after being slightly offended.
explanation.definitionFit: Numb describes being dazed and deprived of feeling, as when stunned or shocked.

clue.text: State of Massachusetts, north of Louisiana and West Indies

indicators.note: in a down entry, north of means placed above, so earlier in the column

parts.note: MA is the postal code for Massachusetts
LA is the postal code for Louisiana
WI is the abbreviation for West Indies

explanation.surface: A geography lesson placing an American state above others.
explanation.walkthrough: 'State' looks like a US state, but the answer is an African country.
explanation.definitionFit: Malawi is a nation in southeast Africa, and a sovereign country is a state.

clue.text: Random: a western where burro's tail removed

indicators.note: removed means that letter is taken out of the word
the tail is the end, so only the final letter is used

explanation.surface: A cowboy film in which a donkey loses its tail.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Western' looks like the film genre but is the adjective; a burro is a small donkey.
explanation.definitionFit: Something accidental happens by chance, without plan, which is what random means.

clue.text: Newspaper redesign 'a bit old'

indicators.note: a redesign reworks a layout, so the quoted letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: A paper's new look is dismissed as dated.
explanation.definitionFit: A tabloid is a small-format popular paper, a kind of daily news publication.

clue.text: He'll ask your opinion about students' placard

indicators.note: about means around, so one word surrounds the other

parts.note: L for learner, twice for plural

explanation.surface: A campaigner wants feedback on a sign the students made.
explanation.definitionFit: A pollster conducts surveys, questioning people about their views.

clue.text: Sip cocoa regularly with utensil; essentially … this?

definitions.text: Sip cocoa regularly with utensil; essentially … this?

indicators.note: regularly means at even intervals, so every other letter is kept

parts.note: first, third, fifth and seventh letters

indicators.note: the essence is the core, so only the central letter counts

explanation.surface: What do you use to sip hot chocolate?
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue is the definition too: a spoon is the utensil you would sip cocoa with.
explanation.definitionFit: A spoon is the obvious implement for taking small mouthfuls of a hot drink.

clue.text: Religious leader's timeless talk

indicators.note: less means without, so the abbreviation for time is dropped

parts.note: to rabbit is British slang for chatter on at length

explanation.surface: A cleric's sermon seems to go on forever.
explanation.walkthrough: In Britain to rabbit, or rabbit on, is to talk endlessly; take its T away.
explanation.definitionFit: A rabbi is a Jewish scholar and teacher who leads a congregation.

clue.text: Primarily: private, sibilant surreptitious tone?

indicators.note: primarily means firstly, so the opening letter of each following word is used

parts.note: initial letters of the four words

explanation.surface: A description of a hushed hissing sound to catch someone's attention.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue is the definition too: the noise is quiet, hissing and secretive.
explanation.definitionFit: Psst is the hushed hiss people make to attract attention discreetly.

clue.text: Was familiar with, reportedly, parameters of Mornington Crescent

indicators.note: reportedly means as spoken, so a word is chosen for its sound
parameters are boundaries, so only the edges of the word are kept

parts.note: the first two and last two letters

explanation.surface: Someone recalls knowing a London Tube stop, or the radio game named after it.
explanation.walkthrough: Mornington Crescent is a London Underground station; here the two words split, the first giving its outer pairs of letters and the second the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: A new moon grows into a thin crescent shape in the sky.

clue.text: Moneylender's yard covered with dodgy merchandise

indicators.note: covered with means wrapped inside, so one piece goes within the other

parts.note: schlock or shlock is shoddy, cheap goods
Y is the abbreviation for yard

explanation.surface: A lender's courtyard piled high with suspect goods.
explanation.walkthrough: Shylock is the moneylender in Shakespeare's The Merchant of Venice, which the word 'merchandise' quietly echoes.
explanation.definitionFit: Shylock is the usurer in Shakespeare's play and has become a byword for a lender.

clue.text: Restoration of Titian urged, showing lack of appreciation

indicators.note: restoration means reworking an old painting, so these letters are remade in another order

explanation.surface: An art lover insisted a Renaissance painting be restored, which earned no thanks.
explanation.walkthrough: Titian was the Venetian Renaissance painter.
explanation.definitionFit: Ingratitude is failing to be thankful, the absence of gratefulness.
